During the whole of a dull, dark, and soundless autumn day, I had been riding alone on horseback through a dreary stretch of country. <break time="0.8s" /> At last, as the evening shadows drew on, I found myself within view of the gloomy House of Usher, the home of my old friend. <break time="0.8s" /> I do not know why, but with the first glimpse of the building, a feeling of unbearable gloom filled my spirit. <break time="0.8s" /> I looked upon the bare walls, the empty, eye like windows, and a few white trunks of dead trees, and my heart sank. <break time="0.8s" /> Hoping to change the sad effect of the scene, I rode my horse to the edge of a black, silent tarn beside the house. <break time="0.8s" /> But looking down at the upside down image of the house in the water, I felt a shudder even stronger than before. <break time="0.8s" /> Its owner, Roderick Usher, had been one of my closest companions in boyhood, but many years had passed since our last meeting. <break time="0.8s" /> Recently a letter had reached me from him, in which he wrote of an illness of body and mind and begged me to visit him. <break time="0.8s" /> Studying the house more closely, I noticed a barely visible crack, which ran from the roof down the wall in a zigzag line into the dark water.

A servant took my horse, and another, who walked silently, led me through many dark and winding passages to the room of his master. <break time="0.8s" /> Never had a man changed so terribly in so short a time, and I could hardly believe that this pale figure was my old friend. <break time="0.8s" /> His skin was deathly pale, and his eyes shone with a strange light, his silky hair floating wildly around his face like a web. <break time="0.8s" /> He suffered from a sickness of the senses, so that only the plainest food and the softest clothes were bearable to him. <break time="0.8s" /> The scent of every flower troubled him, even faint light hurt his eyes, and only a few sounds from stringed instruments did not fill him with horror. <break time="0.8s" /> I shall perish in this terrible folly, he said, for I fear not danger itself, but the feeling of terror that it brings. <break time="0.8s" /> He also told me about his beloved sister, the Lady Madeline, his only companion for many years, whose long illness had puzzled her doctors. <break time="0.8s" /> While he was speaking, she passed slowly through a distant part of the room, and, without having noticed me, she disappeared. <break time="0.8s" /> That very evening she gave in to her illness, and I learned that I would probably never see her alive again.
